newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOFT EMU SEEN MAKING MONETARY POLICY LESS CERTAIN.
newsitem.headline: SOFT EMU SEEN MAKING MONETARY POLICY LESS CERTAIN.

text.p: How do you conduct a single monetary policy for a large and diverse group of European economies? The answer, say many economists, is with great care.

As speculation grows that the euro will be launched in 1999 with perhaps as many as 11 nations, attention is turning towards how a European Central Bank will effectively manage the money that will flow through these countries.

"There is a greater risk of heterogeneity in monetary, inflation and real conditions which will mean that some countries at some point will be unhappy with monetary policy," says Peter Kenen at Princeton University, New Jersey.

Unlike any monetary union that has preceded it, the European version will cobble together a patchwork of economies where the rate of unemployment and the way in which people use money differs considerably.
For example, tiny Luxembourg boasts a jobless rate of only 3.7 percent whereas neigbouring France comes in near the top of the European league at 12.6 percent.
Spain, meanwhile, has the EU's highest rate of joblessness at 20.8 percent and also a large share of youth unemployment.
More specifically, for the proper functioning of monetary policy, how people spend and hold cash also differs from country to country.
Economists note that in Germany roughly 43 percent of the population hold cash in the form of bank deposits. The average Dane leaves only about 11 percent of his money in the bank.
Italians, meanwhile, put a relatively large share of their funds in real assets, such as housing, or in securities.
What this implies for monetary policy is by no means clear, but some say it will make the response of consumers and businesses to interest rate changes much less predictable.

"Changes in short-term rates will have different effects on different banking systems and therefore different impacts on these various economies," says Juergen von Hagen, economist at Bonn's Centre for European Integration Studies.

For the governing board of the ECB, which will operate under a strict mandate of price stability, the dilemma will be how to run a policy that is both credible to financial markets and responsive to the varying demands of its constituencies.

From an economic standpoint, central bankers argue that it will not be the job of the ECB to spur jobs growth, for example. Europe's unemployment problem is structural in nature and can only be remedied through government policies which address the costly regulations many firms are saddled with, they say.

Yet to argue that monetary policy can operate in a political vacuum is as much a fantasy as the idea that a few extra billion euros will put a dent in the 18 million unemployed across the EU, argue other economists.

The makeup of the Frankfurt-based ECB itself will pose challenges in implementing a consistent policy given that it will include representatives which are appointed by the national governments taking part in the euro.

Unlike the members of the Federal Reserve system in the United States, ECB policy-makers will have much closer ties with their electoral roots and may therefore be more susceptible to national influences.
"The question is whether (Italian central bank governor Antonio) Fazio becomes more Italian when he goes to Frankfurt than when he sits in Rome," said a London economist.
"The answer, I'm afraid, is that nobody knows."
Although many expect that the ECB will strongly resist any political interference, it is nonetheless difficult to imagine that it will be able to insulate itself entirely.

Debate over a more balanced approach to economic policy-making within the euro area is already hotting up in the aftermath of the Socialist victory in France, with the new government arguing for a political counterweight to the ECB.

While there may be merit in France's belief that monetary policy should not be too rigidly focused on price stability, economists say it may also reflect national tendencies which will only be exacerbated under a broad monetary union.
"The more heterogenous the union becomes the more national considerations will come to the forefront in the thinking of the (ECB) council," added von Hagen.
